issues.legal_issue: Income derived from property dedicated to a public religious purpose is eligible for exemption when the property is subject to a legal obligation for that purpose, even without a formal trust document.
material_facts: The institution was accepted as religious, and its income-tax exemption claim was considered under the provisions governing income from property held for religious or charitable purposes.
Followers’ offerings were used to acquire property for the common purpose of furthering the institution’s religious objects.
The properties were recorded in the name of the Central Council, and the spiritual leader claimed no title or beneficial interest in them.
The properties had been used for the religious community, and revocation of the trust would not return them to the spiritual leader.
issues.conclusion: The income was entitled to exemption under sections 11 and 12 of the Income Tax Act, 1961; the Tribunal was justified in allowing the claim.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 11 and 12 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, exemption requires that the income be derived from property held under a trust or other legal obligation for charitable or religious purposes benefiting the public, and that the income be applied to those purposes as required by the Act. No formal document is necessary to create a trust. The court relied on The Secretary of State for India in Council v. Radha Swami Sat Sang, 13 ITR 520, and applied the test in All India Spinners’ Association v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay, 12 ITR 482. It distinguished the Privy Council’s decision in Patel Chhotahhai v. Jnan Chandra Bask, AIR 1935 PC 97, because that case considered different statutory requirements.

predicates.income_tax_exemption_proceeding: A person or institution sought exemption for income derived from property in an income-tax proceeding.
predicates.property_subject_to_religious_legal_obli: The property was subject to an obligation requiring its use for religious purposes.
predicates.property_used_for_public_religious_purpo: The property was used to further religious purposes benefiting a religious community or the public.
predicates.no_private_beneficial_interest: The person managing or leading the institution claimed no personal beneficial interest in the property.

issues.definition: When an exemption proceeding concerns property legally obligated and used for public religious purposes, with no private beneficial interest, the income qualifies for religious exemption.

issues.legal_issue: A tax authority should not change a settled determination about a fundamental fact in later assessment years when the parties allowed that determination to stand and no material change justifies a different view.
material_facts: In earlier proceedings, the tax authority accepted that offerings and property were held for religious purposes and allowed exemption; an exemption was also allowed on appeal for a later year.
For subsequent years, the institution’s refund applications were accepted on the basis that its income was exempt until the tax authority changed its position.
The tax authority then assessed the institution on a different basis, although the court found no material change justifying a different view of the fundamental facts.
The earlier determinations had not been challenged in a way that displaced the position they established.
issues.conclusion: Although strict res judicata does not apply to income-tax proceedings and each assessment year is a unit, the settled position on the fundamental facts should not have been changed in the absence of a material change; the contrary assessments could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Each assessment year is a separate unit, and strict res judicata does not apply to income-tax proceedings. However, when a fundamental aspect common to several years has been determined and the parties have allowed that position to stand, it is not appropriate to change it in a later year without a material change. The court relied on T.M.M. Sankaralinga Nadar & Bros. v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, Madras, 4 ITC 226; Hoystead v. Commissioner of Taxation, 1926 AC 155; and Parashuram Pottery Works Co. Ltd. v. Income-Tax Officer, 106 ITR 1, concerning finality in quasi-judicial proceedings.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment_proceeding and fundamental_fact_decided_in_prior_assessment and prior_position_allowed_to_stand and no_material_change

predicates.income_tax_assessment_proceeding: A tax authority determined a person's or institution's liability in an income-tax assessment proceeding.
predicates.fundamental_fact_decided_in_prior_assess: A fundamental fact relevant across assessment years had been determined in an earlier assessment.
predicates.prior_position_allowed_to_stand: The parties allowed the earlier determination to stand without successfully challenging it.
predicates.no_material_change: No material change in the relevant circumstances justified a different determination in the later assessment.

issues.definition: When an income-tax assessment concerns a fundamental fact previously determined and left standing, and no material change has occurred, the tax authority must not adopt a contrary position.
